items.title: Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New Orleans
items.summary: A cruise ship carrying approximately 130 people began sinking in New Orleans after being struck by a tanker while docked. All passengers and crew were accounted for, though 32 individuals were hospitalized with non-critical injuries.

also.title: Cruise Ship Capsizes After Tanker Collision in New Orleans
also.note: Bloomberg's headline specifies that the ship capsized, whereas the BBC describes it as sinking.

also.author: Costas Paris
also.title: A Tanker Lost Control and Hit a River Cruise Ship in New Orleans
also.note: The Wall Street Journal highlights that the tanker lost control prior to the collision.

brief.what: A tanker collided with the docked cruise ship American Heritage on the Mississippi River, causing the vessel to take on water and begin sinking. Emergency responders rescued approximately 130 people from the scene, and 32 individuals were transported to local hospitals with non-critical injuries following the impact.
brief.who: The incident involved the cruise ship American Heritage and an unidentified tanker vessel. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno acted as the primary spokesperson, confirming that all passengers and crew members were safely accounted for after the collision.
brief.context: The collision occurred on a Friday while the American Heritage was stationary at a dock in New Orleans, Louisiana. This section of the Mississippi River is a high-traffic maritime corridor for both commercial shipping and tourism.
brief.why: Authorities are currently investigating the specific cause of the accident, though initial reports suggest a possible steering fault on the tanker may have been the primary factor. Mayor Moreno described the lack of missing persons as a miracle given the severity of the footage.
brief.next: The investigation into the collision remains ongoing as officials work to determine the exact mechanical or human errors involved.

items.title: What we know about the ground stop and what to do if you're affected
items.summary: The FAA lifted a four-hour nationwide ground stop caused by a failure in an aging analogue air traffic control system. The disruption led to thousands of flight cancellations and highlighted a projected $50 billion need for infrastructure modernization.

also.author: Joel Rose
also.title: What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stop
also.note: This headline provides a general status update similar to the BBC.

also.author: Joel Rose
also.title: Old tech blamed for the ground stop that caused flight chaos: 'It got overloaded'
also.note: This framing focuses specifically on the technical failure and the age of the infrastructure.

also.title: Nationwide FAA ground stop lifted but cancellations, significant delays to continue: Transportation secretary
also.note: This headline highlights the ongoing economic and logistical impact on travelers despite the stop being lifted.

brief.what: The FAA implemented the longest nationwide ground stop since 2001, resulting in nearly 8,000 cancelled flights and over 8,500 delays. The stoppage lasted more than four hours before skies were reopened on Friday evening.
brief.who: US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin managed the response, while major carriers including Delta, United, and American Airlines worked to resume operations.
brief.context: This event represents only the second such nationwide stoppage since the 2001 terrorist attacks, exceeding the impact of a similar 2023 failure in the Notam system.
brief.why: Secretary Duffy stated that an incredibly old analogue telecommunications system became overloaded with data following the introduction of new technology. Officials ruled out a cyber-attack, noting that the legacy routers and switches simply failed under the data load.
brief.next: A ripple effect of delays is expected to continue for several days as airlines attempt to clear the backlog of stranded passengers. Duffy indicated the air traffic control system requires a complete overhaul to prevent future occurrences.

items.title: Nissan reduces petrol car production as EV sales boom in China
items.author: Jasper Jolly
items.summary: Nissan is cutting petrol car production in China to accelerate its transition to electric vehicles after a sharp decline in regional sales. The manufacturer lowered its global sales forecast as it faces a harsh market and intense competition from local rivals.

also.author: Kosaku Narioka
also.title: Nissan, Back in Red, Cuts Sales View on China Slump

note.Wall Street Journal: Highlights the company's return to a loss-making status to emphasize financial performance over the production strategy shift.

brief.what: Nissan lowered its global sales forecast to between 2.97m and 3m units and announced a reduction in petrol car manufacturing in China. This move follows a 32% sales decline in the Chinese market during the first nine months of the year.
brief.who: Nissan and its Chief Executive Ivan Espinosa are pivoting strategy to compete with Chinese EV manufacturers who benefited from significant government subsidies.
brief.context: As the world's largest automotive market, China is experiencing a rapid shift toward electric and hybrid cars, contrasting with slower transitions in North America and Japan. Nissan's current Chinese lineup, centered on the petrol-heavy Sylphy family, has struggled to keep pace with local rivals.
brief.why: Espinosa claims the market is very harsh due to intensifying competition and a faster-than-expected shift to new energy vehicles. The company was caught out by a brutal price war and a product mix that remained too reliant on internal combustion engines.
brief.next: Nissan intends to export some products and ramp up its N series of electric and plug-in hybrid models. It is also seeking to ensure its Sunderland and Japanese production qualifies for proposed Made in Europe subsidies.

items.title: US aviation regulator lifts order that grounded thousands of flights
items.summary: The US aviation regulator lifted a grounding order that had halted thousands of flights across the country. The disruption was caused by a temporary telecommunications outage that forced airports to stop take-offs.

brief.what: The US aviation regulator lifted a grounding order that had previously halted thousands of flights across the United States. This action followed a temporary telecommunications outage that had forced airports to stop all scheduled take-offs.
brief.who: The primary actor is the US aviation regulator, which manages flight safety and issued the grounding order. Airports were the secondary actors, as they were required to halt take-offs during the outage.
brief.context: The grounding occurred in the context of a technical failure within the aviation infrastructure. This failure necessitated a complete halt of departures to ensure safety during the period of system instability.
brief.why: The disruption was caused by what the regulator described as a temporary "telecommunications outage." This specific technical issue prevented the normal flow of information required for flight operations.

items.summary: The global oil market remains well-supplied with crude despite ongoing attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran continues to target vessels more than eight months into the regional conflict.

brief.what: The global oil market is currently characterized as being brimming with crude oil supplies despite the persistence of physical attacks on transport vessels. This high level of supply remains a dominant market condition even as smoke continues to billow from tankers targeted in the region.
brief.who: Tehran is the main actor identified as pressing ahead with a campaign of repeated attacks against oil tankers. These actions are being carried out against maritime targets involved in the transport of crude oil.
brief.context: These incidents are taking place near the Strait of Hormuz, which is a vital maritime chokepoint for the international energy trade. The attacks are occurring more than eight months into the conflict described as the Iran war.
brief.why: According to the report, Tehran is continuing its repeated attacks on tankers, yet these disruptions have not prevented the oil market from remaining well-supplied. The article suggests that the market's current state of being brimming with crude persists in spite of the ongoing hostilities.
